fixtures.text: Shipgate is a merge-queue service for monorepos that keeps main green without slowing teams down. In a 6-week trial across 3 repositories with 40 engineers, broken-main incidents fell from 11 to 2, and median time from pull request to merge dropped from 4 hours to 50 minutes. The architecture has 3 parts. First, a speculative batching engine groups up to 8 pull requests and tests the merged result once. Second, a flake quarantine reruns only the 2 percent of suspicious tests instead of the whole suite. Third, a policy layer encodes the 5 merge rules each team already follows, so no workflow changes are needed. Integration takes about 20 minutes: install the GitHub app, select the 1 protected branch, and keep the existing 1200-test suite untouched. Pricing is 12 dollars per engineer per month with unlimited builds. The roadmap has 2 phases: support for 4 more CI providers, then predictive conflict detection trained on 50000 historical merges. The risk is overstated AI claims, so every prediction ships with a measured precision number from the trial data.

fixtures.text: We study whether small rerankers can match large judges for citation-grounded answers. Our corpus has 9000 question-answer pairs across 6 domains, each judged by 3 annotators with 81 percent agreement. The method has 2 stages. First, a 140-million-parameter cross-encoder scores 50 candidate passages per question. Second, a consistency filter drops the 12 percent of answers whose citations do not entail the claim text. Results: the small reranker reaches 78 percent citation precision versus 80 percent for the 70-billion-parameter judge, while running 40 times faster at 3 dollars per million queries instead of 120 dollars. Limitations are 2-fold. Annotator agreement falls to 64 percent on the 2 most ambiguous domains, and the filter hurts recall by 5 points on long answers over 400 words. Future work adds multilingual evaluation in 4 languages and a public leaderboard with 2000 held-out questions. All numbers come from the frozen evaluation split dated March 2026.

fixtures.text: Neighborhood repair cafes keep household goods alive, but organizing one is paperwork chaos. Coordinators juggle volunteer schedules, spare-part inventories, liability waivers, and follow-up surveys across an average of 6 spreadsheets and 3 group chats. Our field study followed 8 repair cafes over 4 months and 24 events, logging 600 repaired items from 900 visitors. The most common repairs were lamps, kettles, zippers, and bicycle brakes, with a 67 percent fix rate and a median repair time of 35 minutes. Fixfolio replaces the spreadsheet pile with one shared workspace. Volunteers pick shifts from a board with 5 roles per event. The parts shelf tracks 300 consumables with low-stock alerts at 20 percent remaining. Visitors sign one waiver that covers all 12 annual events, and the exit survey takes 40 seconds with 3 questions. Organizers told us the real win is institutional memory: when the 2 founding volunteers left one cafe, the playbook preserved all 14 recurring procedures. Pricing is free under 50 visitors per event and 29 dollars per month above that. The plan is to reach 200 cafes in 18 months with 2 full-time staff.
